origin_region: Sơn La · Bắc Yên · Tà Xùa
processing: Shan tuyết leaf from high mountain trees and younger plantings, made mostly as green tea, with white tea also sold by local producers.
harvest_season: Spring picking is usually the most valued, as with other high mountain shan tuyết.
appearance_dry: Long, twisted leaf with pale downy buds.
taste_profile: A mild astringency at first, then a deep sweet aftertaste, with a honey-like aroma and a scent of mountain herbs.

brewing.notes: Hot water and many short steeps suit the big leaf, as with other shan tuyết.

vintage_note: Sold through small producers and brands such as Tafood's Mây range, generally as the current year's tea. Green lots are best within about a year. Prices split sharply between ordinary shan tuyết and buds from old trees, so check which you are buying.
description:
Tà Xùa is a high commune in Bắc Yên district, Sơn La, known for cloud-covered ridges and one of Vietnam's most talked-about groves of old shan tuyết trees. The ancient trees are concentrated around Bản Bẹ.

The tea grows at up to nearly 1,800 metres. Most of the tea is made as green, though local brands have added white teas, including products recognised under Vietnam's OCOP scheme.

The cup is described as gently astringent, then deeply sweet, with honey and mountain herbs in the aroma. Treat it as a big-leaf mountain tea, with hot water and many short steeps, and it will hold up well.

The important buying point is that tea from Tà Xùa is not automatically ancient-tree tea. Of about 300 hectares reported in the commune, only about 40 hold old trees. Ask for traceability, and do not pay old-tree prices for a plain commune name.
history:
The grove around Bản Bẹ holds nearly 3,000 trees reported as 100 to 300 years old, and it has been recognised as a Heritage Tree site. The trees long predate any market for them: reports say the local Hmong did not previously produce tea commercially.

The brand is recent and still being built. Local companies have taken the tea to national and overseas buyers, and the province has pushed products such as Trà xanh Mây towards higher OCOP ratings.
